title: Ollama in Houdini: 60 VEX Tests on a 16GB RTX 5070 Ti
author: Alicia lu
summary: Originally published by Alicia on 2 November 2026 at Digital Garden . Original measurements and limitations are retained. A local Ollama endpoint worked from Houdini 22, but fast VEX replies were often wrong. In 60 frozen trials on an RTX 5070 Ti, Qwen2.5-Coder 7B and 14B each passed 5/30 first attempts. With at most two compiler or semantic feedback repairs, they reached 8/30 and 11/30. I kept all 156 generated snippets unchanged. This is a controlled point-attribute study in headless Houdini 22.0.429 , using owned synthetic fixtures. It does not measure an open garden viewport, artist productivity, production assets, or every local code model. Codex assisted the implementation, execution, checks and writing; the counts come from saved native results. What actually ran The machine was Windows 11, Ryzen 9 9950X, 64 GB RAM and an RTX 5070 Ti with 16,303 MiB reported by driver 617.42. Houdini ran its own Python 3.13 through hython ; the API bridge required only Python's standard library. Ollama was 0.13.2 , with CUDA 13 selected by its own runtime. I retained that version for this study rather than installing the downloaded updater. I started a separate Ollama service at http://127.0.0.1:11435 , with a dedicated model directory, one parallel request and one resident model. The ordinary default port is 11434. These scripts use 11435 deliberately and do not change the workstation's global Ollama or proxy settings. Tested model Quantization Registry size, bytes First correct Correct after ≤2 repairs qwen2.5-coder:7b-instruct Q4_K_M 4,683,087,561 5/30, 16.7% 8/30, 26.7% qwen2.5-coder:14b-instruct Q4_K_M 8,988,124,298 5/30, 16.7% 11/30, 36.7% These are the two models tested, not a recommendation or a claim about the newest model releases. Full manifest digests and /api/show responses are in the reproduction package. For reference, the pinned digest prefixes are dae161e27b0e and 9ec8897f747e . Ten tasks, frozen before inference The formal plan records SHA-256 hashes of the task specification and native validator before model inference. Each model saw ten tasks with seeds 11, 23 and 47: 30 trials per model . Task order rotated identically for both models. Settings were temperature 0.2, top-p 0.9, context 8192 and at most 768 generated tokens per attempt. The tasks were a height mask, height-driven color, safe normal normalization, an integer-ID scale pattern, radial smoothstep fade, a specified right-handed Y rotation, root-pinned wind, a sine terrain height, point-group membership and bounding-box UVs with a zero-extent fallback. Every constant and convention appeared in the prompt. These are mathematical attribute exercises inspired by plant work, not tasks extracted from the production garden. Each snippet ran unedited in a point Attribute Wrangle against three fixtures: a 45-point grid, 37 deterministic jittered points and nine edge cases. The last fixture includes a degenerate X bounding box; normals include zero vectors. Time was fixed at frame 13 and 24 fps, giving @Time = 0.5 . An independent Python oracle checked the requested values within absolute tolerance 2e-5 , tuple widths, finite values, point count, preserved inputs and unrequested attributes or groups. All three fixtures had to pass. Ten known-correct controls passed first; four deliberately wrong controls covering values, position changes, extra attributes and syntax were rejected. The prompt prohibited loops, geometry creation/deletion, I/O, channel references and external geometry. A single code fence could be removed; the code inside was not repaired by hand. Failure feedback contained native compiler messages or numeric mismatches, capped at 3500 characters. There were at most three attempts in the same conversation. I call the second result success after feedback , because these are dependent repair attempts. It is not the independent-sampling pass@k estimator, and three seeds per task are too few to establish broad model rankings. Compiling and being correct are separate checks On first attempts, 7B compiled on all fixtures in 7/30 trials but was correct in 5/30. The 14B model compiled and passed in 5/30. A compile-only check would have accepted two extra 7B failures. Failures included undefined unprefixed variables, invented function calls and incorrect attribute assignment. One 7B height response declared a local height_mask , attempted point(...).y without resolving the overloaded return type, and modified P despite being asked to preserve it. Some repair attempts repeated the same faulty code. A rotation response called rotate as if it accepted and returned a point vector; Houdini rejected that signature. The terrain task passed all three first attempts for both models. Neither model solved the radial fade, root-pinned wind or UV task in any of the three repair trials. That is a result for these exact prompts and checks, not evidence that local models can never solve those tasks. The larger model added six repaired successes after its five first-attempt successes; 7B added three. A plausible-looking snippet and a fast answer were insufficient grounds to apply code to an active scene. Latency and memory Metric 7B 14B Median first response after warm-up 0.474 s 0.865 s Median first nonempty streamed token 66.3 ms 79.4 ms Median summed model-response time per task, including repairs 1.553 s 2.461 s Ollama resident allocation after load 4.975 GiB 10.118 GiB Separate cold warm-up wall time 32.068 s 2.031 s The first two latency rows use all 30 first attempts per model, including failures. Summed response time includes model requests but excludes native validation and interaction time. Ollama's prefix caching remained enabled, and these snippets were short. This is not a fresh-process startup measurement for every request. The cold warm-ups were separate setup observations. Model order and system state differed, so the 32-second versus two-second observations do not establish a general load-time advantage for 14B. The memory numbers are /api/ps size_vram divided by 2³⁰. They are Ollama resident allocation, not total driver peak or spare viewport capacity . A parallel 200 ms nvidia-smi logger produced malformed CSV rows because its asynchronous appends were not serialized. I preserved that failed diagnostic and excluded it from driver-peak claims. Both models unloaded successfully afterward, with an empty /api/ps model list. No Houdini GUI responsiveness conclusion follows from this headless study. The Python client that worked in Houdini Ollama's chat API returns text in message.content ; the generate API uses response . Both can stream. For a small blocking client, explicitly disable streaming: import json import urllib.request import urllib.error API = " http://127.0.0.1:11435 " opener = urllib . request . build_opener ( urllib . request . ProxyHandler ({})) def chat ( model , messages , timeout = 180 ): body = { " model " : model , " messages " : messages , " stream " : False , " keep_alive " : " 5m " , " options " : { " temperature " : 0.2 , " num_ctx " : 8192 , " num_predict " : 768 }, } request = urllib . request . Request ( API + " /api/chat " , data = json . dumps ( body ). encode ( " utf-8 " ), headers = { " Content-Type " : " application/json " }, ) try : with opener . open ( request , timeout = timeout ) as response : data = json . load ( response ) except urllib . error . HTTPError as error : raise RuntimeError ( f " Ollama HTTP { error . code } : " + error . read (). decode ( " utf-8 " ) ) from error if data . get ( " error " ): raise RuntimeError ( data [ " error " ]) if not data . get ( " done " ): raise RuntimeError ( " Incomplete response " ) return data [ " message " ][ " content " ], data The direct opener matters on this workstation: the inherited Python proxy configuration did not bypass 127.0.0.1 . A controlled GET to /api/version returned 502 through the inherited opener and 200 with version 0.13.2 through the direct opener. The change is scoped to this loopback client; it does not disable the user's OS proxy. I also reproduced three distinct failure cases in native Houdini Python: Test Actual result Correct handling Read reply["response"] from a successful chat response KeyError: 'response' Read reply["message"]["content"] Call json.loads on the entire streamed generate body JSONDecodeError: Extra data Parse individual lines, or request stream: false Request an intentionally missing model HTTP 404 with an error body Report the HTTP error before reading a text field Those are local reproductions. They do not establish what caused an error in somebody else's tutorial. The streaming documentation describes the newline-delimited response contract. Apply code through a checked controller For the formal experiment, a controller set snippet on a point Attribute Wrangle, requested its geometry and checked the native result. A Python SOP also made a real localhost request and returned READY while preserving 60 input points. The separate demonstration replayed the accepted, unedited 14B color snippet from formal trial 1: float t = clamp ( @ P . y / 1 . 5 , 0 , 1 ); @ Cd = lerp ( set ( 0 . 05 , 0 . 20 , 0 . 03 ), set ( 0 . 80 , 0 . 30 , 0 . 10 ), t ); The editable HIP was saved and reopened, and its point count and color attribute were read back. Its saved Python SOP replays the verified HTTP reply instead of automatically starting inference on opening. The figure is a plot of native point data with a linear-to-sRGB display conversion, not a viewport screenshot. Synchronous HTTP calls block the Python cook until completion. I did not test a threaded GUI controller here. A production tool needs its own UI handling, timeouts, cancellation and scene-specific validation; this package demonstrates the bounded headless path. FAQ Can a local model write working Houdini VEX? Yes, some snippets passed native semantic checks. Both tested models passed 5/30 first attempts; feedback increased the totals to 8/30 and 11/30. Does 14B fit on this 16GB card? It loaded with a reported 10.118 GiB Ollama resident allocation during this headless study. An open production scene and responsive viewport were not tested. Why does /api/chat produce KeyError: 'response' ? A successful chat response uses message.content . I reproduced the wrong-key exception. Streaming parse failures and HTTP errors are separate cases. Does this code upload the scene? The tested client sends only the declared messages and options to loopback. It does not serialize geometry or call a cloud inference endpoint. Model downloads are a separate network operation; this is not a complete workstation network audit. Should I paste generated VEX into my active garden? These results support checking it in an isolated scene first. Even compiling was not sufficient to prove correctness in this task set. Data and reproduction Download the reproduction ZIP , analysis JSON , all-attempt CSV and README . The package includes the frozen prompts and validator, every request and response, separate setup/integration failures, model metadata, figures and editable HIP. Model weights and user settings are excluded. Related measured work: RTX 5070 Ti in Houdini , Claude Code versus Codex for Three.js and procedural Houdini plants for the web . title: Agentix Lite v0.8.1: Can You Audit a Linux Security Prototype from an Android Phone?
author: jackymenCZ (jackymenCZ)
summary: A security prototype, 110 passing tests, real local socket experiments, 12 Observer findings, and one important rule: a passing test is not a production deployment. Thank you for your support! Every test, every bit of feedback, and every conversation helps move this project forward. https://www.npmjs.com/package/sentinel-ir-mcp/v/0.3.0 Repository: "Agentix Lite at commit ddf626d" ( https://gitlab.com/jakubrojicek11/agentixlite/-/tree/ddf626d1c3e9a7f4b2ee91d019f7c624266b4c2d/ ) https://www.npmjs.com/package/agentixlite/v/0.8.1 The 30-second version What happens when you try to audit a Linux security prototype using an Android phone? I spent this audit testing Agentix Lite v0.8.1 in Termux. We examined its event pipeline, UNIX socket authentication, reputation engine, SQLite storage, TCP honeypot, MCP interfaces, Shadow Observer, and systemd integration. The complete Python test suite reported 110 passed. A real local TCP-to-engine experiment passed 8/8 checks. The watchdog integration experiment passed 5/5. We also found 12 Observer issues and several deployment limitations. One important detail: this was a prototype tested on Android/Termux, not a production VPS deployment. No real production firewall enforcement or seven-day server observation was claimed. Now let's unpack what those numbers actually mean. Part 1: The 2-minute explanation for everyone What is Agentix Lite trying to do? Imagine a small security guard for a Linux server. It watches incoming activity, looks for suspicious behavior, evaluates the source, and records what happened. Its basic architecture looks like this: A sensor notices something suspicious. It creates a small event describing what happened. The event travels through a local UNIX socket. The main engine evaluates the event and updates reputation. The result is stored in SQLite. In Shadow Mode, the system can recommend an action without actually blocking anyone. That final point matters. Shadow Mode is observation, not enforcement. The system can say: "This IP looks suspicious. It would qualify for a temporary ban." But it does not have to touch the firewall. Think of it as a fire alarm being tested without actually flooding the building with water. What did we test? We did not just inspect Python functions and declare victory. We created temporary databases, local sockets, separate processes, synthetic events, and a local TCP connection. One experiment followed this complete route: TCP connection → honeypot listener → authenticated UNIX datagram → EventReceiver → Agentix Engine → SQLite. The actual TCP connection came from the local IPv6 loopback address "::1". Then we injected a separate synthetic event using "8.8.8.8" to verify the Shadow Mode decision. The results: The real TCP event reached the engine. The loopback address was not turned into a ban candidate. The synthetic external address became "BAN_CANDIDATE". No real firewall operation happened. Both actors remained stored in SQLite. Result: 8/8 checks passed. Why not just say it works? Because there is a difference between a working prototype and a production security system. Our tests ran on Android through Termux. We did not install Agentix on a real Debian or Ubuntu VPS during this audit. We tested many internal mechanisms, but we did not prove how the whole system behaves under real server traffic, real systemd supervision, or long-term operating conditions. That distinction is not a weakness in the report. It is the point of the report. Part 2: The 8-minute developer deep dive Test environment and scope The audit was performed against the local repository at: Commit: ddf626d1c3e9a7f4b2ee91d019f7c624266b4c2d Version: Agentix Lite v0.8.1 Platform: Android / Termux Architecture: aarch64 Python: 3.13.13 Node.js: 26.3.1 Go: 1.26.4 Python tests used an isolated virtual environment. The repository remained clean throughout the audit. No application source code was changed as part of these experiments. Temporary databases, sockets, test directories, and synthetic inputs were used to isolate the test runs. Full Python suite The complete repository test suite reported: 110 passed, 1 warning in 14.23s The warning concerned the deprecation of the current HTTPX integration with Starlette's TestClient. It was not a failed test. The targeted experiments below were separate test runs. Their counts should not be added together as though they represented one unique global test suite. Core engine and reputation We examined event validation, pattern detection, reputation scoring, and engine decisions. The component-level checks included: Component| Result Detection, events, patterns, reputation| 16/16 Engine integration with temporary SQLite and FakeFirewall| 13/13 Storage and ghost actor behavior| 10/10 RollingBuffer| 5/5 One important test used a fake firewall: class FakeFirewall: def init (self): self.batches = [] def block_many(self, ips, timeout_seconds): self.batches.append((list(ips), timeout_seconds)) return FirewallResult(len(ips), len(ips), 0) This allowed the engine's decisions to be observed without applying real firewall rules. For Shadow Mode, a synthetic honeypot event from an external IP was expected to produce: BAN_CANDIDATE The fake firewall remained untouched. This distinction is important when testing security software. We want to verify decision logic without accidentally turning an experiment into a real blocking operation. SQLite, WAL, and bounded storage Storage testing covered: SQLite persistence. WAL behavior under sustained reading. Capacity pressure. Ghost actor admission and eviction. IPv6 fingerprint handling. Rolling event buffers. Two important experiments showed why configured limits must be interpreted carefully. In one WAL test: Configured hard limit: 1 MiB Observed physical WAL: 1,050,632 bytes In another: Configured hard limit: 256 KiB Observed physical WAL: 276,072 bytes The logical write guard rejected additional work, but the physical WAL file could exceed the configured threshold. This means the guard is useful for controlling application-level storage pressure. It should not be advertised as an exact physical filesystem limit. That is a small but important wording difference. UNIX sockets and authenticated event delivery Agentix separates telemetry into three ingress lanes: Normal events. Honey critical events. Host critical events. The receiver enables Linux peer credential passing: sock.setsockopt( socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_PASSCRED, 1, ) It extracts the credentials from the received ancillary data and checks the sender UID against the expected identity for the lane. This is more meaningful than trusting an event's JSON field claiming to be from a particular service. We also tested concurrency, queue limits, and per-IP fairness. One initial concurrency assertion expected 60 accepted host events. The actual configured per-IP queue limit produced 32. That was a test expectation error, not proof of a product defect. We corrected the interpretation and separately exercised fairness and rate limiting. A real local TCP-to-engine experiment The end-to-end experiment used an actual local TCP listener and the existing honeypot implementation. The observed event included: source = honeypot_port ip = ::1 path = tcp/ The receiver reported: received: 1 queued: 1 credential_rejected: 0 listener_errors: 0 The engine then processed the event and persisted the actor. A second synthetic event from "8.8.8.8" was used to verify the external ban-candidate decision. Final result: PASSED: 8 FAILED: 0 TOTAL: 8 No real firewall rules were changed. One honeypot limitation We also tested a failed telemetry delivery. The honeypot listener updates its per-IP cooldown before sending the event. The telemetry client performs one non-blocking send and does not retry. If the receiver is missing, the event is lost, but the cooldown is still consumed. A second connection from the same IP during the cooldown therefore does not generate another event. This was reproduced with a controlled local experiment. Finding: "HONEYPOT-001". It is an event availability limitation, not evidence of a firewall bypass. MCP interfaces and runtime truth We tested the Python MCP server and the Go gateway separately. Results included: Area| Result Python MCP STDIO| 16/16 Go gateway unit tests| 6/6 Go gateway HTTP checks| 15/15 Go gateway STDIO checks| 13/13 The gateway's health endpoint checks whether the runtime status exists, whether its process is alive, and whether its status is stale. However, we found an important runtime reporting issue. MCP-STATUS-001: Enforcement status is not authoritative The Go gateway's shadow summary hardcodes: mode = shadow enforcement_enabled = false It does not derive these values from an authoritative daemon runtime snapshot. The Python MCP interface reads its own process configuration, which is not necessarily the same thing as the running daemon's actual state. An AI client could therefore receive an inaccurate description of the system's enforcement state. A read-only interface still needs trustworthy status data. Read-only does not automatically mean reliable. Shadow Observer: twelve findings The Observer reads runtime status, storage metrics, system information, service state, and optional MCP health. It writes measurement samples to JSONL. It does not directly change firewall rules or Agentix configuration. We tested its coverage calculations, counters, restart handling, malformed data, schema versions, and timestamps. The audit identified twelve findings: ID| Finding| Why it matters OBSERVER-001| Drop counters can be double-counted| Inaccurate loss reporting OBSERVER-002| Malformed JSONL lines are silently skipped| Missing evidence can go unnoticed OBSERVER-003| Failed systemd inspection can appear as empty data| Service state may be misrepresented OBSERVER-004| Disabling observation during a later installer run does not explicitly stop an already enabled timer| Possible unexpected sampling OBSERVER-005| Service restarts are recorded but do not generate anomalies| Operational explanations can be missed OBSERVER-006| Controller-level firewall shedding is not independently classified as an anomaly| Some firewall losses can remain unnoticed OBSERVER-007| Structurally invalid JSON records can crash reporting| One bad record can break a summary OBSERVER-008| Unknown schema versions are accepted| Compatibility is not guaranteed OBSERVER-009| Future timestamps can pass coverage checks| False evidence of observation OBSERVER-010| Agentix version changes are not flagged| Mixed-version measurements go unnoticed OBSERVER-011| Numeric and ISO timestamps are not cross-validated| Contradictory time information is accepted OBSERVER-012| Duplicate timestamps can make counter calculations order-dependent| Reports can become nondeterministic These findings have different levels of operational importance. They are not twelve security exploits. Example: duplicate timestamps We deliberately created two input files containing samples with an overlapping timestamp. The same records in a different file order produced different counter deltas: Input order A: events delta = 1100 Input order B: events delta = 2100 The report accepted four records with three unique timestamps and raised no anomaly. This matters because monitoring output should be deterministic when the underlying evidence is identical. Example: coverage is not health We also tested stale, unknown, and stopped runtime states. The time coverage gate could still be true even when runtime health was not good. That is not necessarily a violation of the gate's narrow definition. It means operators must never interpret: coverage_gate = true as: the system was healthy Those are different claims. Deployment and systemd checks The deployment review covered: "deploy/setup.sh" "systemd" service and timer units runtime directory creation Docker configuration UNIX socket permissions nftables preflight MCP binary architecture watchdog integration The installer passed its shell syntax check: bash -n deploy/setup.sh The runtime directories are created through: systemd/agentix-tmpfiles.conf The Honey API container is configured to run as UID "65534", with the Agentix group added. The receiver expects the Honey sender UID to be "65534". The design is consistent on paper, but the full Docker-to-host socket delivery was not tested on a production VPS. Watchdog integration The main systemd service declares: Type=notify NotifyAccess=main WatchdogSec=30s The engine derives its heartbeat interval as half the configured systemd watchdog timeout. For a 30-second timeout: Expected heartbeat interval = 15 seconds The main loop calls: engine.periodic_cleanup(receiver) even when there are no events. During idle periods it waits for 20 milliseconds before continuing. We then tested the actual engine heartbeat through a local UNIX notification socket. Results: PASS | Watchdog interval is half systemd timeout PASS | Engine sends watchdog heartbeat PASS | Engine sends status after heartbeat PASS | Heartbeat is throttled between intervals PASS | Heartbeat is sent again after interval PASSED: 5 FAILED: 0 TOTAL: 5 This verifies the local engine-to-notification path. It does not replace a live systemd deployment test. Deployment limitations discovered Architecture mismatch The bundled gateway is: bin/agentix-mcp-linux-amd64 ELF 64-bit LSB x86-64 The Android test environment is: aarch64 The native validator includes both x86-64 and ARM64 builds, but the Go MCP gateway currently has only the AMD64 binary in this checkout. The installer checks whether the binary is executable, not whether its architecture matches the host. This could cause the MCP service to fail on an ARM64 VPS if enabled with that binary. Existing nftables table The installer applies the nftables ruleset only if the Agentix table does not already exist. If an older table exists but lacks one of the expected sets or chains, the preflight can fail rather than automatically reconciling it. That is safer than silently assuming the firewall is correct, but it is an installation and upgrade limitation. Android runtime path The prototype uses: /run/agentix/status.json In our Termux environment "/run" did not exist and the write failed with: errno 30: Read-only file system Writing to a temporary writable directory succeeded. The Linux deployment installs a systemd tmpfiles configuration to create "/run/agentix" and its subdirectories. Therefore, this Android failure is an environment difference, not proof that the Linux deployment has the same problem. Final verdict Agentix Lite v0.8.1 has a substantial amount of locally tested functionality. The audit demonstrated: Event processing and reputation decisions. Authenticated local event transport. SQLite persistence and capacity handling. A real local TCP honeypot-to-engine path. Shadow Mode behavior without real firewall operations. Python and Go MCP interface tests. Watchdog integration logic. A set of reproducible Observer edge cases. But there is a boundary we must respect. This was a prototype tested in Termux on Android. It was not a production VPS audit. We did not perform: A live Debian/Ubuntu systemd deployment. A real production Docker-to-host socket integration. A real nftables enforcement test. A 24-hour Shadow Mode observation. A seven-day observation period. A DDoS-resilience assessment. The next meaningful validation step is a dedicated Debian/Ubuntu AMD64 VPS running Agentix in Shadow Mode, with enforcement disabled. Collect real runtime evidence, explain anomalies, inspect candidate-ban precision, and only then consider further operational claims. No automatic enforcement should be enabled just because the local test suite is green. A green test suite is a useful signal. It is not a production certificate. Experiment first. Headline second.

title: How to Hire a Python Developer in 2026 Without Hiring the Wrong One
author: Ayesha
summary: How to Hire a Python Developer in 2026 Without Hiring the Wrong One If you need to hire a Python developer in 2026, you have already run into the central problem of this market: every resume says "Python." A bootcamp graduate who wrote three automation scripts says Python. A data scientist who has never deployed a web app says Python. An engineer who has run Django in production for six years also says Python. These are not the same hire, they do not cost the same money, and picking the wrong one costs you weeks of onboarding before the mismatch becomes obvious. This guide gives you a hiring process that filters for what you actually need. The Python Hiring Mistake Almost Everyone Makes Most job posts read like this: "Looking for a Python developer. Must know Python, Django, Flask, FastAPI, Pandas, TensorFlow, AWS, Docker." That post will attract everyone and qualify no one. It signals to strong engineers that you do not know what you need, and the best candidates — the ones with options — skip it. Python is not one job. It is a language stretched across at least six different professions, and a developer who is excellent in one is often mediocre in another. Hiring starts with naming which Python you need. There Is No Generic Python Developer — Only Clusters Here are the clusters you will actually encounter: Django developers build full web applications — admin panels, user accounts, billing pages. If your product is a classic web app with a database behind it, this is your cluster. FastAPI and Flask developers build APIs and backend services. FastAPI development has become the default for new API work in 2026, and this cluster is what most "we need a backend developer" posts actually mean. Data engineers and analysts live in Pandas, NumPy, and SQL. They move and clean data. They usually cannot build you a web app, and you should not ask them to. Machine learning engineers train and serve models. This cluster commands a real premium in 2026 because every product roadmap now has an AI feature in it. Automation and scraping developers write scripts with BeautifulSoup, Scrapy, Playwright, and Selenium. This is honest, useful, cheaper work — I built a production screenshot API on Python, Flask, Selenium, and Docker myself, and it is a completely different skill from training models. DevOps-adjacent Python developers write the glue: CI/CD scripts, Lambda functions, infrastructure tooling. Before you write a single word of your job post, pick one cluster. If you genuinely need two, hire for the harder one first. Step 1 — Write a Job Post That Names the Cluster A job post that attracts the right people names four things: the framework, the production surface, the deployment target, and what the hire will own in the first 90 days. Compare these two openings for the same role: Weak: "Python developer needed for backend work. Must know Django, REST APIs, and AWS." Strong: "We need a FastAPI developer to own our billing API — roughly 2 million requests a month, Postgres on RDS, deployed with Docker on AWS. First 90 days: take ownership of the webhook pipeline, add idempotency, and get our test coverage from 40 percent to 80 percent." The strong post does three things: it names the cluster (FastAPI APIs), it names the scale (so seniors self-select in and juniors self-select out), and it names the actual work (so the candidate can picture the job). Strong engineers apply to specific problems, not to the word Python. Step 2 — Screen for Production Experience, Not Tutorials Resumes lie by omission. Git history tells the truth. When you hire a Python developer, spend twenty minutes on their public work before any call. Look for repositories with migrations, tests, a Dockerfile, and CI configuration. That combination means the code was meant to run somewhere real. A repo with only Jupyter notebooks or forked tutorial projects means the code was meant to be looked at. A quick check you can run on any candidate repo: git log --author = "candidate-name" --since = "12 months ago" --oneline | wc -l ls Dockerfile docker-compose.yml requirements.txt pyproject.toml 2>/dev/null Why it works: sustained commits over months signal real maintenance, and the presence of Docker plus dependency files signals the code was deployed, not just written. Then, in the interview, ask for one production story: "Walk me through the last time a Python service you owned went down. What did the logs say, and what did you change?" You are listening for specifics — a real traceback, a real query that locked a table, a real config mistake. Vague answers like "we restarted the server and it was fine" tell you this person has never owned a system at 2 a.m. Follow up with: "Where do secrets live, and how do they get into the running container?" Anyone who has shipped will answer in one sentence. Anyone who has not will wander. Step 3 — Use a Paid Trial Task That Mirrors Real Work Unpaid take-home tests filter out every senior with options. Pay for four to six hours of the candidate's time at their rate, and make the task mirror the actual job. A paid trial is the single most reliable filter when you hire a Python developer sight unseen. For a FastAPI development role, a task that works looks like this: build one endpoint that accepts a signup payload, validates it, rejects duplicate emails with a proper 409, and is covered by at least one test. Show the candidate what "good" looks like without writing their solution for them. This is the shape of a production-grade FastAPI endpoint: from fastapi import FastAPI , Depends , HTTPException , status from pydantic import BaseModel , EmailStr app = FastAPI () class SignupPayload ( BaseModel ): email : EmailStr password : str def get_user_store (): # Injected dependency: trivial to swap for a test double. return UserStore () @app.post ( " /signup " , status_code = status . HTTP_201_CREATED ) async def signup ( payload : SignupPayload , store = Depends ( get_user_store )): if await store . email_exists ( payload . email ): raise HTTPException ( status_code = 409 , detail = " Email already registered " ) user = await store . create ( payload . email , payload . password ) return { " id " : user . id , " email " : user . email } Why it works: validation happens at the boundary with Pydantic, the database is hidden behind an injected dependency so the route is testable, error cases return explicit status codes, and no ORM internals leak into the HTTP layer. When you review the submission, do not grade on cleverness. Grade on exactly these four things: does it validate input, can you test it without a database, are errors explicit, and would you let this run on your infrastructure? One more rule for the trial: give every candidate the same task and the same time box. You are comparing engineers, not tasks. If the role is really about building an API rather than hiring long-term, read how custom REST API development is scoped and priced first: https://webixyhub.com/blog/custom-rest-api-development-cost-hiring-guide Django vs FastAPI vs Flask — Match the Hire to Your Stack Clients often ask which framework their hire should know, as if there is a right answer. There is not — there is only the answer that matches your codebase. Django is the right choice for admin-heavy products where the built-in admin, ORM, and auth save months. FastAPI is the right choice for modern APIs, especially when type safety and automatic docs matter. Flask is the right choice for small services and embedded tooling where Django would be overhead. The hiring implication is simple: do not hire a Django specialist to build your FastAPI service because FastAPI is trending, and do not reject a strong Flask developer for a Django role if they have shipped real products. Frameworks are learnable in weeks. Production judgment is not. If you are weighing Python against PHP, my guide to hiring a Laravel developer covers the same vetting process from the other side of the stack: https://webixyhub.com/blog/hire-laravel-developer-guide What It Costs to Hire a Python Developer in 2026 Rates vary by cluster, seniority, and geography, but the structure of pricing is stable. Freelance rate guides for 2026 report a global average of roughly 61 to 80 dollars per hour for a Python freelancer, with senior offshore engineers typically landing between 2,500 and 3,500 dollars per month for dedicated remote work. Three things move the price: the AI overlap premium (anyone who can both build the backend and integrate or serve models costs more, because they replace two hires), the depth of production experience (someone who has owned uptime costs more than someone who has written features), and the engagement model (a dedicated monthly developer is cheaper per hour than the same person on short contracts). Do not optimize for the lowest rate. A mid-priced developer who ships in three weeks is cheaper than a cheap developer who ships in three months. If a quote is dramatically below the ranges above, you are not getting a bargain — you are getting someone else's learning curve on your budget. Red Flags That Should End the Conversation "I can learn it" at senior prices. Willingness to learn is great in a junior. In a senior billing senior rates, it means you are funding their education. No production story. If a candidate cannot describe a real outage they debugged — the traceback, the dead end, the fix — they have never owned a system. Tutorial-only GitHub. Forked courses with no original commits, no tests, no deployment artifacts. Everyone starts somewhere, but you are not hiring potential at senior rates. Secrets in code. If their sample project commits a .env file or hardcodes an API key, their security habits are disqualifying no matter how clean the code looks. Cannot explain deployment. "I push to GitHub and it works" is not a deployment story. You want to hear about the pipeline: build, test, image, deploy, migrate, roll back. Fixed price for undefined scope, no questions asked. A developer who quotes without interrogating your requirements has not thought about where the work actually is. For AI and ML claims, one extra check: ask how they would serve the model — batch or realtime, and what latency budget they would design for. Hand-waving here means the "ML experience" was a notebook, not a system. If your product takes payments, the integration work deserves its own vetting — webhook handling alone has ended launches: https://webixyhub.com/blog/fix-stripe-webhook-signature-verification-failed-laravel The One-Week Interview Loop Day one and two: review their public work asynchronously using the checks above. Day three: a 45-minute call built around one production story and the secrets question. Days four and five: the paid trial task, same task for every candidate. Day six: review the submission against the four grading points and make the decision. This loop respects the candidate's time, which matters because the engineers you want are evaluating you at the same time. Slow, multi-round gauntlets with unpaid homework select for candidates with no better options. A fast, paid, realistic process selects for professionals. Final Checklist Before You Send the Offer You named the cluster in the job post. You verified production experience in their git history. You heard a real outage story. You ran the same paid trial for every finalist and graded it on validation, testability, explicit errors, and deployability. You checked the rate against the market instead of chasing the lowest bid. If that sounds like more process than you want to run to hire a Python developer, there is a simpler option: work with someone who has already done it. I build production Python and Laravel systems — custom Python API development, automation, payment integrations — for clients who would rather ship than interview. You can see the work and get in touch at https://webixyhub.com .

title: About 30% of public PX4 drone logs have a GPS delay setting more than 50 ms off, and EKF2's own residuals agree
author: munimv2
summary: PX4's state estimator, EKF2, has to know how old each GPS sample is when it arrives. Up to PX4 v1.17 that is the parameter EKF2_GPS_DELAY , 110 ms by default. Almost nobody changes it: in the public flight logs we read, 96-98% of vehicles ran the default. So we measured it. We took random samples of real flights uploaded to PX4 Flight Review since October 2025, one log per vehicle, and wrote down every prediction before downloading anything. How the delay is measured gps_lag.py compares two things that should tell the same story. One is the change in GPS velocity between consecutive GPS samples. The other is the IMU's acceleration, rotated to north-east and integrated over the same interval, shifted back by a candidate lag. The lag where they fit best is the GPS delay. It reads no position, so no location leaves the log. Hover-only flights don't move enough to measure, so they don't pass its gates. What the fleet says First sample: 164 logs from 115 vehicles. Median lag 99.8 ms, close to the default. But 29.6% of logs were more than 50 ms off their own setting. Two logs from the same vehicle agreed to a median 5.3 ms, so this is a property of the vehicle, not noise. Replication: 98 logs from 98 other vehicles. Median 113.8 ms; 31.2% more than 50 ms off. Both figures fell inside ranges written down before the run. Does EKF2 agree? A measured lag is only useful if it means something to the filter. EKF2 logs its GPS velocity innovations, the difference between what it predicted and what the GPS said. If the GPS is later than the filter thinks, the innovation should lean in a predictable direction whenever the vehicle accelerates. We pre-registered that check, and the first run failed as written: strong agreement, but with the opposite sign. The plan had assumed the textbook innovation sign, measurement minus prediction. PX4 computes prediction minus measurement ( _state.vel - velocity in gps_control.cpp ). We didn't regrade after seeing the data. We applied the written rule, withdrew our suggested setting, published why, and pre-registered the corrected check on the 98 fresh logs, whose innovations nobody had read. It held. On 89 validated logs: the two methods rank the logs alike (Spearman +0.86 ); in 25 of 27 logs more than 50 ms off their setting, EKF2's residuals lean the same way. So the tool again offers the measured lag as a starting value for the delay setting when it is more than 50 ms off. Check it with EKF2 log replay before flying it. Agreement in direction and rank is not a calibration. Does it matter to the filter? EKF2 accepts or rejects each GPS velocity sample with an innovation test: a test ratio above 1 means rejected. We pre-registered whether a wrong delay shows in that ratio, on a third, fresh sample of 256 logs ( mismatch-2026 ). It shows. While the vehicle accelerated, the ratio was a median 2.7 times its steady-flight value on logs more than 50 ms off their setting, against 1.7 times on the others. The larger the mismatch, the larger the rise. Rejections: 20% of mismatched logs had at least one GPS velocity sample rejected in flight, against 16% of the others. That gap is within chance, but the interval reaches +14 points, so our own "no extra rejections" check failed. We can't say a wrong delay is harmless. Does the receiver model matter? PX4 records which GPS receiver it detected in every GPS message's device id. ArduPilot's u-blox driver gives M8, M9 and F9 the same 120 ms, with the comment that the F9 figure is "not verified yet from flight log". On three sets of PX4 vehicles with none in common, the u-blox M9 came out far less late than the F9P and the M8 (median lag, number of vehicles): M9 F9P M8 first receiver sample (163 logs) 71 ms (25) 143 ms (16) 147 ms (15) earlier samples, receiver read afterwards (213 logs) 76 ms (32) 144 ms (27) 151 ms (7) fresh sample, November (298 logs) 81 ms (29) 143 ms (42) 145 ms (12) M9 − F9P was −67 ms (95% interval −101 to −48) and then −62 ms (−88 to −42). The F9P and the M8 were within 8 ms of each other every time, as ArduPilot assumes. But every study's own enough-data check failed, each time on the M8 (12 turned up in the fresh sample against 15 needed), so by the rules we wrote in advance this is still exploratory . And a default per receiver model would barely help: the spread within each class is wide, so it would put only 2.3 points more vehicles within 50 ms of their real lag. Knowing the model doesn't replace measuring your own vehicle. It isn't the measurement rate. We read each log's actual rate from the receiver's own time stamps ( GRADE-rate.md , pre-registered). On the same 125 ms grid, M9 logs were still 53 ms less late than the other u-blox logs (interval −106 to −19 ms). One of our own predictions failed, and the reason is worth knowing if you fly an F9P: since PX4 v1.16, the driver asks an M9 for 10 Hz and an F9P L1L2 for 5 Hz (PX4-GPSDrivers bbdd576 , January 2025). Before that it was 8 Hz and 10 Hz. Our plan had read the older driver. EKF2's GNSS innovations on real flights PX4 RFC #28837 argues, from a simulation, that EKF2 treats every GNSS sample as independent although real GNSS errors stay correlated, which leaves the filter's normalised innovations tiny and its gate far too wide. We measured that on 285 real flights from the same fresh sample ( nis-2026 , pre-registered): the typical log's position NIS was 0.0079 , where a consistent filter gives 0.693; velocity 0.024 ; in units of the innovations' real spread, the 5-sigma gate is about 30 sigma wide for position and 17 for velocity (the RFC's simulation: more than 11); position innovations stay correlated for a few seconds (0.78 at 1 s, 1/e after about 3.7 s); velocity ones fade within about a second. These are EKF2's innovations, not raw GNSS errors, and they are logged every 500 ms, so the limits are in the grade. If you fly PX4 v1.18: the delay is now per receiver PX4 v1.18 removes EKF2_GPS_DELAY ( PX4 PR #26660 ). Each receiver now gets its own delay, SENS_GPS0_DELAY and SENS_GPS1_DELAY (110 ms by default, matched to a receiver through SENS_GPS0_ID / SENS_GPS1_ID ). The sensors module moves each sample's timestamp_sample back by that much, and EKF2 fuses the sample at that time. Old values are migrated on upgrade. On PX4 main the parameters are already renamed SENS_GNSS0_DELAY and SENS_GNSS1_DELAY , and vehicle_gps_position becomes vehicle_gnss ( PR #24399 ). The fresh sample had 8 logs from v1.18 pre-releases. None has EKF2_GPS_DELAY , and in all 8 the sample times were moved back exactly 110.0 ms. On one of them, with an NMEA receiver, the measured lag was 187 ms, 77 ms later than the delay applied. The PR's motivation is multi-receiver setups. Our numbers suggest the receiver model alone matters too. A vehicle with an M9 and an F9P may want two quite different values, and a per-receiver parameter is now where they go. Measure your own vehicle rather than copying our medians. While we were in there: flight health px4-log-health reads the same logs for the things Flight Review shows by eye: vibration, accelerometer clipping, GPS jamming and spoofing, battery warnings, failsafes and motor saturation. On 208 public flights from 208 vehicles, 75% raised at least one flag. One finding surprised us. Flight Review colours the vibration plot green, orange and red at 4.9 and 9.8 m/s². But PX4 v1.12 and older computed that metric from delta velocities, in m/s, about 200 times smaller. On those logs the bands don't mean anything, and old logs look quiet when they aren't. Among v1.13+ logs, 51% sit in orange or red. Version 0.2.0 reads the release from the log and doesn't band old ones. We've described this in Flight Review issue #352 . One report per flight: in your browser, on the command line or in CI checkup.py puts both together: one short Markdown report per log with the health flags, every figure placed among those 208 public flights, and a GPS delay verdict that measures the lag, compares it with the log's delay setting and checks the direction against EKF2's innovations. It suggests a value only when the lag is more than 50 ms off and the innovations don't disagree. Since version 0.3.2 it also reads PX4 v1.18 logs: it takes the delay EKF2 applied from the log's own sample times and names the SENS_GPSn_DELAY to change. Here is a real report on three public logs . In your browser, with nothing uploaded: munimv2.github.io/px4-log-check runs checkup.py in Pyodide on your own computer (version 0.3.1 for now). Pick a .ulg and the report appears. On the three sample logs it gave a report identical to the command line's. If you keep test-flight logs in a repository, the same report can land in every CI run's job summary: - uses : actions/checkout@v4 - uses : munimtechnologies/px4-log-health@v0.3.2 with : logs : " **/*.ulg" Or on the command line: pip install numpy pyulog requests git clone https://github.com/munimtechnologies/px4-log-health && cd px4-log-health python fetch_deps.py # gps_lag.py and innov.py from px4-gps-lag, pinned commit python checkup.py flight.ulg # or: python health.py flight.ulg / python gps_lag.py flight.ulg Everything is open: the plans written before each run, the grades, and one line per log (vehicle ids hashed, no positions). GPS delay grades: GRADE-innov-confirm.md , GRADE-innov.md (the sign mistake), GRADE.md , mismatch-2026 Receiver model: GRADE.md , GRADE-confirm.md , GRADE-rate.md , GRADE-fresh.md EKF2 innovations: nis-2026 Fleet health: GRADE.md Limits: these are uploaded logs, often uploaded because something went wrong, so they are not the rate in the air. The model is first-order, and both methods share the attitude estimate. Receiver classes are as PX4 detected them; the M8 class is small. Data: PX4 Flight Review public logs (Dronecode / PX4, CC BY 4.0). Code Apache-2.0; text CC BY 4.0. Disclosure: the analysis, the code and this post were made with AI agents working in the name of MV2 of Munim, Inc.

title: GLiNER2 vs an LLM: I tested both on 640 labelled examples
author: Ahmad Dogar
summary: My comparison of LLMs, Jev and CDMs was all reading: docs, papers and vendor numbers. It left me wanting something I could run myself. GLiNER2 is that thing. It is an Apache-2.0 extraction model from Fastino that runs on a CPU, and you give it a schema, not a prompt. So I ran it on this laptop against Claude Haiku 5.5, with 640 labelled examples. I could not find an independent head-to-head for JSON extraction, which is the part I care about most. The short version: GLiNER2 is very fast and fine when the answer is written plainly in the text. Haiku was more accurate on every test but one, and the gap gets wide as soon as a value needs judgment. Percent correct. Entities are F1, and invoices count a note as right only if all four fields are. What I tested News topics: 200 AG News articles, 4 labels. Banking intent: 200 BANKING77 questions, 77 labels. Named entities: 200 CoNLL-2003 sentences, scored on exact type and text. Invoices: 40 notes I wrote myself, 20 easy and 20 hard, with four fields each. The GLiNER2 side ran on an M1 Pro with 16 GB of memory, CPU only, one text at a time. I tried three models: gliner2.5-small-v1 , gliner2.5-base-v1 and GLiNER2.5-Decide , which is the classification specialist. Getting it running takes a few lines: pip install 'gliner2[local]' from gliner2 import AutoExtractor m = AutoExtractor . from_pretrained ( " fastino/gliner2.5-small-v1 " ) print ( m . extract_json ( " Invoice 4471 from Acme Roofing, total due $1,240.50 by 12 March 2026. " , { " invoice " : [ " vendor::str " , " number::str " , " total::str " , " due_date::str " ]}, )) {'invoice': [{'vendor': 'Acme Roofing', 'number': '4471', 'total': '$1,240.50', 'due_date': '12 March 2026'}]} The results All scores from the same samples on one run. Decide was the slowest model and did not clearly beat base on classification, so I would not reach for it based on these two sets. Speed and memory M1 Pro, 16 GB, CPU only, one text at a time. Time grows with the number of labels, which is worth knowing before you hand it a long taxonomy. There is no Haiku column on purpose. I ran Haiku through the Claude Code CLI, and its start-up time would make any latency number meaningless. For cost, the billed tokens at Haiku's list price of $0.10 and $0.50 per million work out to roughly $0.05 to $0.16 per 1,000 calls depending on the task. The CLI may add some tokens of its own, so treat that as an upper estimate. Where it broke The hard invoices show the difference best. These are real shapes of mistake from the base model: Five real misses from the base model. Some of this is not a fair fight. GLiNER2 pulls text out of the input, so it cannot produce $300.00 when that number is not written anywhere. Four of my 20 hard notes need a value like that, so a perfect score was never possible for it. The other misses are a different problem: it picked the wrong value, or filled a field that should have been empty. The last row bothers me most. A model that fills a missing field with something plausible is harder to catch than one that returns nothing. Tuning did not rescue it. Dropping the confidence threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 left the invoice score unchanged and lowered entity F1 from 53.4% to 50.6%. Giving it the same field definitions Haiku got moved hard invoices only from 9 to 10 of 20: schema = { " invoice " : [ " vendor::str::Who issued the invoice " , " invoice_number::str::The current invoice number " , " total_due::str::What is still owed now, after credits and payments " , " due_date::str::The current date it must be paid by " , ]} Same mistakes again My last post quoted a paper finding that LLM fallbacks tend to repeat a cheap model's confident errors. I saw a version of that here. Of Haiku's 33 wrong banking answers, GLiNER2 base got 32 wrong too. On news it was 17 of 20. Some of those are probably ambiguous or debatable labels, and I did not check them one by one, but it means a second model is not a free safety net. How far to trust this I wrote the invoices. Forty notes is small, and I wrote both the notes and Haiku's prompt, so 40 of 40 is not a general claim about Haiku. One run, default settings. I did not fine-tune GLiNER2, which is one of its selling points. Training on your own data could change these numbers. Exact matching is harsh on entities. CoNLL also has a lot of sports tables, which is an odd test for any model. The label wording matters. 35 of base's 61 news errors were science and technology articles labelled business, so better label names might help. No Jev or CDMs here. I did not run them, so this says nothing about how they compare. Which one I would use GLiNER2 base when the value is stated plainly, the volume is high, or the text cannot leave your machine. Check that a missing field stays empty. An LLM when the answer needs reading: balances, superseded dates, or anything where a wrong value costs you money. Small only when memory or speed really is the limit. It lost three easy invoices that base got right. Before switching anything, label 200 of your own examples and run this same comparison. My invoices are not your invoices, and an afternoon of labelling is cheaper than trusting my table. Originally published on my site . More posts and projects at mahmadmanzoor.com .

title: Multiple House Properties Under The Income-tax Act 2025
author: Dadas Nikita
summary: Owning than one house has become very common these days. You may have one house where you live with your family another house that you bought as an investment and maybe a third house that you got from your parents or grandparents. Some people buy a house in another city because of their job while others buy extra houses to earn money from rent or to build wealth over time. Even though owning properties can be a good financial decision it also means you have more tax responsibilities. Many people think that all the houses they own are treated the way under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Others think that if a house is empty or only used sometimes it does not affect their taxes. These ideas can lead to mistakes when you file your Income Tax Return.

title: WorkBuddy or Codex? Choose by the Work You Need Done
author: weiyi
summary: If most of your work involves documents, spreadsheets and presentations, I’d start with WorkBuddy. If you spend your day changing code, investigating errors and running tests in a project directory, I’d start with Codex. Both can write code and handle files. The useful question is where your work starts and what you need to take away. “Which is smarter?” won’t get you far. The main difference is the workflow WorkBuddy is Tencent’s general-purpose AI workspace. Its official capabilities include research, documents, spreadsheets and presentations, as well as website and application development. Give it a set of materials and specify the output you need: that is a natural way to use it. Codex has terminal, IDE and cloud entry points. For local development, it can inspect a project, edit files and run commands with tools already on your machine. Your existing build, test and Git workflows can continue. Task Start with Check Competitor research and reports WorkBuddy Reliable sources and supported conclusions Combining spreadsheets and making slides WorkBuddy No lost fields; usable output files Adding features to an existing project Codex Consistent structure and reasonable changes Fixing bugs, testing and code review Codex Correct diagnosis and verified results A new website or small tool Try either How easily it fits future maintenance This is a suggested division of work, not a limit on either product. Results also depend on the model, permissions and connected tools. If a task fails, check whether it lacked sources, command access or clear requirements before switching products. With WorkBuddy, specify what you want to take away “Analyze competitors” is too broad. You may get lots of text that still needs organizing. Try this instead: Use these three product websites to make a comparison table of pricing, main features and intended users. Cite a source for each item. Mark missing information “unconfirmed.” Finish with three recommendations. Deliver an editable spreadsheet and a one-page summary. Now the materials, scope and format are clear. For spreadsheets, add the deduplication field, currency units and rules for missing values. Every omitted rule leaves another guess to fix later. Split large jobs into two stages: facts and tables first, then the report or slides after you approve the direction. Formatting before checking facts creates unnecessary rework. Save recurring templates and rules in project materials or skills; next time, replace the inputs rather than explaining everything again. With Codex, give it a goal you can check “Optimize the website” can produce a long list of changes without a clear improvement. Be specific: Fix overflowing article tables on mobile. Keep horizontal scrolling and check Chinese and English pages. Explain the cause, changed files and how you verified the fix. For backend errors, provide the trigger, relevant logs and expected behavior. For changes spanning modules, ask it to diagnose the problem and explain its proposed edits before implementing them. Put lasting project rules in AGENTS.md: build commands, directory conventions and deployment steps. Keep it short and useful. You don’t need the most expensive model or strongest reasoning setting for every job. Try faster settings for copy edits, styling and simple batch changes. Increase reasoning for cross-module work, elusive bugs and complex reviews. Exact choices depend on the models currently available. Review the changes and rerun the scenario that failed. “Done” is a notification; code and execution results are the evidence. Using both: make the handoff clean For a blog, WorkBuddy could organize topics, sources and outlines, while Codex handles pages, multilingual structure, APIs and deployment. Assign reports and channel copy according to the output needed. Hand over files, settled decisions, remaining tasks and unverified information. A long chat transcript makes the next tool guess again. Don’t have two agents edit the same code at once. Let one implement while the other reviews without editing, or use separate branches or work directories for parallel development. Otherwise you may have to repair overwritten changes yourself. Which is better value? Don’t compare only subscription fees or response speed. Run three to five recurring tasks and record completion time, usage or fees, and your own correction time. An answer in one minute that takes half an hour to repair costs more of your time than a five-minute result you can check and use. If you want just one tool, pick the one closest to your daily work. Start with WorkBuddy for office materials, Codex for existing code projects. Add the other when you find a concrete gap. Sources checked October 13, 2026. These recommendations use official capabilities, not a comparative hands-on benchmark. WorkBuddy Codex CLI This article was prepared for DEV with AI assistance.

title: The Roadster tempts me. But I'm not putting down RMB 332,000 yet
author: weiyi
summary: My first reaction to the latest Roadster news was: finally, something is happening again. Then I saw the production year. 2028. That's Musk's latest timing, according to an October 16 report from Cailian Press. After all the years since the 2017 unveiling, another date doesn't immediately get me excited. Starting production isn't the same as handing a car to a buyer in China, either. I still want to see the car. As for reserving one now, I'll wait. Who is it for? I wouldn't make it my only car I don't find the likely buyer hard to picture: everyday transport is already covered, and they want something they simply enjoy owning. Take it out on a sunny weekend. Enjoy looking at it in the garage, too. Some people love a Ferrari's sound, others a Porsche's driving feel. There will also be people drawn to Tesla's slightly adventurous approach. At this point, saving electricity isn't really the issue. If my budget also had to cover family transport, commuting and long trips, I wouldn't be considering a Roadster. Those needs would come first. It plays a similar role within Tesla. Model 3 and Model Y sell in volume; the Roadster gives people a reason to think Tesla can still make something surprising. The audience discussing it can be much larger than the audience buying it. The current Chinese reservation information describes the Performance version as a two-seater, with active aerodynamics and a multimode intake system. The old descriptions of a four-seat sports car may no longer match what is being offered. I'd like to know what all that feels like on the road. We aren't at the point where I can answer that yet. RMB 332,000 is a reservation payment. I'm reluctant to queue this early Tesla's Chinese site currently lists an initial payment of RMB 332,000. That's a reservation payment, not the car's price. The frequently quoted US$200,000 and US$250,000 figures were the original 2017 prices for the base and Founders Series versions. With so much time passed and the product changing, converting those figures into a present-day Chinese on-road price doesn't tell me much. This is what holds me back: I can't yet work out the final cost, the specification I'll receive and the delivery date together. RMB 332,000 can buy an everyday car. I'm not keen to exchange it for a place waiting for updates. Other people will be happy to. I understand wanting to join the queue early, particularly if you've followed Tesla and waited years for this car. But I'd read the Chinese reservation agreement before paying, especially the refund process and what changes when it becomes a firm order. An American report saying a deposit is refundable doesn't make the Chinese agreement unnecessary. As for selling it in China, the visible route today is online reservation. My reading is that Tesla can take interest from its keenest buyers first and let the car's publicity draw attention. We don't yet have enough information about Chinese allocations, delivery or final pricing to claim we know its full sales plan. When it comes to buying one, I doubt the salesperson will need to spend long explaining electricity costs per 100 km. I'd spend more time asking where it can be repaired, how long special parts take and what happens if I damage the underbody. An electric sports car needs more than acceleration now In 2017, the Roadster's acceleration figures were memorable by themselves. Today, China already has plenty of very quick EVs. The Yangwang U9 and MG Cyberster occupy different price brackets and offer different experiences, but they show how much choice has grown for an EV with character. I need the Roadster's final price before deciding what to compare it with. If it competes for traditional sports-car money, I'm even more interested in how it drives. One hard launch is impressive. Can it sustain performance for several laps? How are the brakes? Is the steering enjoyable? Those matter more to me than a single demonstration sprint. Then there are the dull questions that could come up every day: will it clear the garage ramp, is the seat comfortable after an hour, and can I replace a damaged tyre without a saga? Buying a toy doesn't mean wanting to spend every day looking after it. Musk's past talk of a SpaceX cold-gas thruster package, even “flying,” is interesting to watch. I wouldn't build that into my valuation yet. Let's see the final Chinese specification and what's permitted on public roads. One detail worth keeping straight: 0–60 mph is acceleration to roughly 96.6 km/h, not 0–100 km/h. Both the date and the units matter when reading this car's specifications. I'd like driver assistance. The Tesla badge doesn't confirm the features You might reasonably ask whether a Tesla this expensive would have FSD. I'd like to know, too. But as of October 16, 2026, the Chinese reservation information I could find did not establish the complete driver-assistance specification, FSD functions or pricing for the Chinese Roadster. Calling it standard equipment, or promising city driving assistance at delivery, is premature. I'm perfectly happy to have assistance in a sports car. After a day out, help following traffic in a jam sounds useful. Easier parking would be welcome, too. Enjoying driving and wanting an easier time in congestion aren't contradictory. But if driver assistance were my main reason to buy, I'd try cars already delivered with their functions enabled. There's no need to imagine the Roadster's future Chinese features for it. Even if supervised FSD is offered, the driver still has to watch the road; it isn't driverless operation. So would I buy one? For now, I wouldn't reserve it. I'd wait for production cars. Once Chinese pricing is available and there's a car to try, I'd happily go and see it. If it's enjoyable to drive and isn't too troublesome to use, there will still be time to get excited. What I'd really like to read now is what the first owners think after a few months. I've seen plenty of Roadster launch news over the years. title: Houdini 22 Gaussian Splats to Three.js: A Native Export Test
author: Alicia lu
summary: Originally published by Alicia on 2 November 2026 at Digital Garden . Original measurements and limitations are retained. Houdini 22 produced a usable web splat, but a successful PLY write was not enough. The native point writer used Houdini attribute names and big-endian binary output. Spark 2.3.1 rejected that byte order. I tested an explicit inverse attribute conversion and a separate, value-preserving endian adapter, then loaded both PLY and SPZ in Three.js. The second fixture went through the official Karma-to-GSplats recipe: 24 rendered views of an owned procedural plant, a 12,000-point initialization, 1,200 training steps and native PLY/USD export. Its PLY was 3,121,605 bytes ; its SPZ derivative was 235,748 bytes . Both displayed 12,000 splats. Native Karma and browser appearance still differed, so this is a verified transfer with documented limits, not a lossless rendering claim. Codex assisted the experiment and writing. The raw data, failed setup records, editable scenes and exact adapters accompany the article. Neither fixture is a photographic capture or the production Digital Garden scene. What is native, and what changed in H22? The Bake GSplats SOP dates to Houdini 21.0 . Houdini 22 adds the ML Train GSplats TOP and the ML Train GSplats from Karma recipe used here. The node called Surface Splat is an unrelated paint-mask tool; its name does not establish Gaussian-splat export support. The workstation was Windows 11, Ryzen 9 9950X, 64 GB RAM, RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB and driver 617.42. Houdini was 22.0.429 with a commercial license. Its isolated training environment installed Torch 2.9.1+cu128 , torchvision 0.24.1+cu128 and gsplat 1.5.3 . The browser lab pinned Three.js 0.186.1 and Spark 2.3.1 ; the production garden dependencies were not upgraded. First check: a controlled round trip I created 120 asymmetric splats along a small helix, with nonuniform scales, Y rotations, opacity 0.85, color and nonzero degree-one SH terms inside a degree-three property layout. Four deliberate contaminants made cleanup testable. This is a numerical control, not a scan-quality example. The File SOP read the standard 3DGS input. Bake GSplats converted it to Cd , linear scale , xyzw orient , restorient , GS_Alpha and three 16-component GS_SPH_* attributes. I enabled SPH coefficients and disabled color linearization for this bounded web round trip. These choices preserve the incoming learned color convention; they are not a universal Houdini display setting. Cleanup stage Rule on this fixture Remaining points Input 120 intended splats plus four contaminants 124 Crop X/Z inside ±0.75; Y between −0.1 and 1.5 123 Alpha Remove GS_Alpha below 0.05 122 Scale Remove a splat with any linear scale component above 0.1 121 Neighbors At least three points, including self, within radius 0.25 120 Those thresholds are fixture-specific. Applying them indiscriminately to a real scan could destroy valid detail. The inverse Python SOP restored scalar f_dc_0..2 , f_rest_0..44 , opacity as a logit, scale as logarithms and rotation as wxyz. It took the DC and higher-order terms from the native GS_SPH_* tuples. The helper rejects an orientation change relative to restorient , rather than pretending it can export arbitrarily transformed SH correctly. For opacity and scale, the relevant inverse operations are: opacity = math . log ( alpha / ( 1.0 - alpha )) log_scale = [ math . log ( component ) for component in linear_scale ] wxyz = [ orient [ 3 ], orient [ 0 ], orient [ 1 ], orient [ 2 ]] The full helper clamps numerical endpoints and is in the package. After native serialization and independent parsing, the maximum scalar difference from the original 120 intended splats was 2.384e-7 . That verifies this cleanup-only round trip, not general transform, gamut or SH-editing behavior. Two different export problems Saving the baked native attributes directly produced GS_Alpha , orient1..4 , scale1..3 and GS_SPH_* properties. A web reader expecting opacity , rot_0..3 , scale_0..2 and f_rest_* does not recover the same splat representation from those names. There was a separate byte-order issue. The native File SOP wrote binary_big_endian PLY. The pinned Radix core reader could decode it, but Spark 2.3.1 returned Unsupported PLY format: binary_big_endian . Houdini's gply -a generated ASCII, which this Radix core reader rejected too. Neither failure means the file was absent or the native cook failed. For Spark, I made a little-endian derivative by swapping each scalar field's byte order and changing the format declaration. Independent parsing verified every value and property name exactly equal before and after that adaptation. It changes no axis, scale, color or coefficient. The native binary originals remain available. The first panel uses an endian-adapted native-attribute file to isolate the schema problem. The middle and right panels use the cleaned 120-splat representation. A loader returning a point count alone did not prove a correct image. One plant through the official Karma recipe The owned source contains a cylinder stem, five double-sided mesh leaves, a spherical flower, simple materials and a dome light. The recipe created a 24-camera Fibonacci sphere. I used 384 × 384 images, increased the camera offset after a clipped-framing pilot, and limited native render concurrency to one job. The useful graph was: IN_Stage loads the source USD. Setup_Camera_Array and the Karma render settings define views and AOVs. TOP rendering writes multipart EXRs containing C/RGBA, albedo, N and depth. ML Preprocess GSplats writes camera metadata, the COLMAP-like dataset and a 12,000-point initialization. ML Train GSplats runs the bounded fit and exports PLY and USD. I kept the setup failures. The headless recipe wrapper tried to access a network-editor UI after creating its nodes. Mixed path separators then coincided with 24 failed file-copy tasks; normalizing the experiment's base directory to forward slashes cleared those failures. A hyphen in owned-plant later caused the native USD prim export to fail after writing the trained PLY. Using owned_plant as the export name fixed the final export. With scripted linked parameters, follow_parm_reference=False was needed to keep that change from also renaming the dataset. The successful final cook reused the rendered dataset and installed environments and took 54.675 seconds . That includes cached graph work, launching, training, validation and export; it is one observation, not an end-to-end installation time or repeated training benchmark. The final native USD reopened as ParticleField3DGaussianSplat with 12,000 positions . Separate portable copies of the source recipe scene and the 120-point round-trip scene were saved and reopened. A real Karma XPU render of the exported USD also completed. The trainer reported 31.303 dB PSNR and 0.97446 SSIM over six validation views after 1,200 steps. Eighteen views supplied photometric training, but the initial depth point cloud used the complete 24-camera array. These are not fully unseen geometry tests, and the black background makes aggregate image scores easier than a foreground-only quality judgment. Leaf color and overlap differences are visible. The export has the SH3 property layout , while the final log says the active trained degree was one : higher bands had not been trained by this 1,200-step schedule. Counting 45 f_rest_* properties is not proof that all those bands contain learned detail. PLY to SPZ, with measured losses I used the MIT-licensed @sparkjsdev/radix 0.0.1 core bundle , pinned locally, to write SPZ v3 with SH enabled. I did not install or test GSOPs. The converter retained the splat count and SH3 layout on decoding the SPZ back. Asset Standard PLY bytes used by Spark SPZ v3 bytes Splats in both Cleaned numerical control 31,432 1,328 120 Karma-trained plant 3,121,605 235,748 12,000 For the plant, SPZ decoding changed position components by at most 0.0001221 scene units , scale by at most 3.175% relative , quaternion angle by at most 0.00805 radians , and SH coefficients by at most 0.003922 in the converter's decoded representation. Opacity matched that representation in this sample. These are quantization observations, not a universal bound for SPZ or proof of perceptual equivalence. The Radix intermediate also has its own packing, so those error figures isolate the decoded intermediate-to-SPZ step rather than proving float-exact retention from the original PLY. The independent native scalar check above covers a different boundary. Browser acceptance The formal browser run had 12 fresh-profile starts : four asset/format cases, three repeats each. Chrome used Spark 2.3.1 with Three.js WebGLRenderer at 960 × 640, DPR 1. After 90 settling frames, each trial recorded 120 RAF intervals: 1,440 intervals in total. Houdini training and Ollama inference were not running during these trials. File Median fetch/decode/setup Median first GPU submission completion Decoded count Control PLY 22.8 ms 281.4 ms 120 Control SPZ 25.8 ms 283.4 ms 120 Plant PLY 35.7 ms 285.6 ms 12,000 Plant SPZ 32.7 ms 283.9 ms 12,000 These are localhost observations from three trials per case, not network delivery measurements. First GPU submission completion is a gl.finish() boundary before the settling period; it does not certify the first complete scene or physical display presentation. All trials stayed visible and had no captured page errors. The median RAF interval was 16.7 ms in every case, at this desktop's roughly 60 Hz ceiling. That does not rank renderer throughput. The actual SPZ display used the normal Spark API: const spark = new SparkRenderer ({ renderer , enableLod : false }); scene . add ( spark ); const splat = new SplatMesh ({ url : ' /assets/trained-plant.spz ' , lod : false }); await splat . initialized ; scene . add ( splat ); At the same static browser camera, plant PLY versus SPZ had foreground-union RGB RMSE 1.100 on an 8-bit scale , over 36,843 pixels. The mask includes pixels where either image differs from its background by more than three channel values. This is a limited image-difference check, not an assessment of all viewpoints. For the native/browser comparison figure, I first corrected my native EXR preview to use the same OCIO configuration and scene_linear → sRGB - Display conversion as training . A simple sRGB transfer without the configured working-space conversion had been misleading. The corrected preview and original failed preview are retained. Remaining color and rendering differences are visible in both the trainer comparisons and cross-renderer views; I have not established a single universal correction for them. FAQ Can Houdini 22 export a standard Gaussian-splat PLY? The training TOP did so here. For edited native SOP attributes, I needed an explicit inverse schema conversion; the native File SOP's big-endian output also needed an adapter for this Spark version. Can I turn a Karma scene into a web splat? Yes, this small synthetic plant completed the official recipe and displayed in PLY and SPZ. It does not establish scan quality, dynamic animation support or suitability for every garden asset. Is SPZ lossless? No. This plant was much smaller on disk, with measured scale, position, rotation and SH differences. Only two static browser views and one formal camera were inspected. Does a point count prove the export worked? No. The raw native schema could be decoded as a tiny point cloud after endian adaptation, while the intended Gaussian sizes and opacity were not represented correctly. Is SH3 fully trained here? No. The file stores the SH3 layout, but only degree one was active at the end of this short fit. Data and reproduction The reproduction package , analysis JSON , browser CSV and README contain the actual outputs and limits. Model installation caches and browser profiles are excluded.
