title: Deploy a Static Site on Alibaba Cloud: Codeup, Flow, OSS and ESA
author: weiyi
summary: Once an article is written, the release process should deliver it reliably to readers. Build, upload, refresh and verification need distinct steps so you can see where a failure occurred. A clear release path This project currently builds and publishes through local commands, uploads static output to OSS and serves it through ESA. Codeup and Flow configuration templates are ready, but the actual repository and cloud pipeline are not connected yet. When configuring Flow later, reuse these steps: Install dependencies from the lockfile with npm ci. Run npm run build to check types and generate pages. Upload static assets first, then publish HTML and Sitemap. Refresh ESA caches and verify that public content matches the build. Notify search engines and save successful submission state. Treat different content differently in the cache Content-hashed assets can be cached for a long time. HTML and Sitemap benefit from revalidation and a refresh after publication so readers don't receive stale content. Cache refresh is asynchronous. Verify that public pages return the new content before submitting URLs, reducing the chance that a search service sees an old page or error response. Make failures recoverable A multi-file OSS upload isn't atomic. If it fails midway, rerunning can complete the missing parts. Search notifications save successful batches, leaving only pending content for a later attempt. A platform accepting a request does not mean an article is indexed. Check website publication and search notifications separately. See the project's deployment documentation for configuration and maintenance details. title: AI is splitting up the work. I'm more interested in who finishes the job
author: weiyi
summary: When I saw that ChatGPT could put several agents to work at once, my first thought was writing for this blog. Checking documentation, finding examples and verifying prices could finally happen in parallel. Then I thought about the results coming back. Someone still has to read them together. Prices are an obvious trap: one agent finds subscription pricing, another finds API pricing. Put those straight into an article and fluent writing won't save it. Add Cursor's cloud-agent update, Google DeepMind's Minecraft experiment and Anthropic's quantum-circuit research, and my question becomes: how much work would these actually save in my own projects? Research in parallel, then sit down and compare the results OpenAI's announcement says GPT-6 Astra Pro in ChatGPT supports parallel agents, with individual progress tracking and completed tasks you can open to review. The announcement explicitly makes it available to Pro users in the Chat tab. I'd try that for a technical article. One agent reads official documentation, another finds examples, another checks pricing and access conditions. That should be quicker than waiting for one agent to do everything in order. But I wouldn't immediately combine their answers into a draft. The web app and API of the same product can offer different capabilities. A fresh announcement might not yet be reflected in the documentation. Each answer can have a source and still mislead readers when placed beside the others. So I'd still ask: which version, what date and which region? Only once those line up would I use the material. Research can happen simultaneously; I don't want to skip that final comparison. With Cursor, environment management is what I'd like to try Cursor's update lets cloud agents build interactive canvases. Finish a dashboard or report, send someone a link, and they can view it. Convenient enough. For development, though, I'm more interested in the beta Environments API: creating and managing agents' cloud environments programmatically. Spending ages on setup before writing any code wears down my patience. The repository is cloned but dependencies aren't right. The service finally starts, then a missing environment variable turns up. Get it working, switch tasks, and start again. Agents need those problems solved, too. If repositories, dependencies and test environments can be prepared and reused, at least each task doesn't have to begin with a conversation about how to start the project. Cursor says large multi-repository environments load five times faster. I'd read that as less waiting before work begins, not a fivefold improvement in the whole development process. The repository limit isn't consistent: the X post says 500, while the changelog and agent-creation API documentation say 300. If I needed that many, I'd plan around the documented 300 and confirm access to a higher limit first. Four agents playing Minecraft: I'd like to see the handoffs Google DeepMind's experiment put four Gemini 4 Argon agents into Minecraft from scratch. They defeated the Ender Dragon after roughly 27 hours. According to the announcement, they operated through code and text, wrote 2,783 programs, divided jobs over chat, shared notes and debugged together, without humans helping them complete the game tasks. But the researcher's full account includes important details. They played on Easy, read their surroundings and acted through Mineflayer, and had a pathfinding plugin. They didn't see game pixels or use a keyboard and mouse like a human. Researchers could monitor, pause or stop the experiment from a dashboard. It wasn't a smooth run, either: 605 respawns, with 22% of programs ending in an error. The log records victory at 27 hours and 14 minutes. “Finished in 27 hours” can hide a lot of retries. The win is worth watching, but I'm more curious about what happened during those hours. When one agent finds resources, how does it tell the others enough to save them unnecessary trips? When something goes wrong, who notices and brings everyone back on track? Development has similar problems. Several agents being able to code doesn't guarantee they'll work well together. One changes an interface while another builds a page against the old version. Put them together and it will still break. For my blog, I'd consider dividing translations by language, or having one agent check links while another checks pages. I'd be much less comfortable with several agents changing styles and routes at once. Each might think its work is finished; the combined result still needs a look. Before deciding whether this transfers well to real projects, I'd also want repeated-run success rates and the cost of those 27 hours. Without them, I can't work out whether it's worthwhile. Knowing whether the result is right matters more to me There's an arrangement I like in Anthropic's quantum-circuit research : give Claude Mythos 5 circuit specifications and an automated evaluator. After a design, a program checks correctness and scores “qubit count × gate count.” The model gets the feedback and tries again. Improvement doesn't depend entirely on the model explaining how well it did. The report says all eight selected tasks produced designs more resource-efficient than the best previously published approaches. One Reed–Solomon decoder used roughly one-twelfth the gates of Google's earlier construction. That's a circuit-design comparison, not a twelvefold speedup of an entire quantum computer. Nor does the research claim no human participation: the point-addition task ran for 53 hours, with an initial brief and occasional human prompts to explore more broadly. Quantum circuits are far from my daily work, but I need ways to check AI's results when building a website, too. If it says a page is fixed, I'd like to see it on a phone. If it says a link is repaired, open it. If it says a release is live, confirm we're seeing the new version. Having those checks makes it easier to delegate more. Otherwise, four “finished” messages just mean asking four times: finished where? Show me. So I'd start these features with a few independent blog tasks. Agree on which files each agent can change and what it should return, then look at the combined work afterward. I'd like them to finish their parts so I can check and use the result. If I still need four or five conversations open to track down who changed what, I'd rather start with fewer agents. This article was prepared for DEV with AI assistance.

title: Same Claude Opus 5.5: Why Some People Ship an App and Others Call It Dumb
author: weiyi
summary: Same model, Claude Opus 5.5. Some people say it gets a week's work done in half a day. Others say it gets two out of every three questions wrong. I recently used it to build a mobile app called Ruzai (如在). When you're away from your computer, it lets you use your phone to view the AI assistant's conversations on that computer, send it messages, and approve the critical actions it wants to run. Product design, UI, code, GitHub Actions pipelines that build Android APKs and push iOS builds to TestFlight, a self-hosted OTA update server, App Store listing assets: nearly all of it was done by Opus 5.5 inside Claude Code. Along the way we switched tech stacks once, evaluated two cross-platform frameworks, and I rejected the UI three times. Looking back, model capability was almost never the bottleneck. With the same model, whether the results are good comes down to the person using it. This post breaks that down into a few concrete gaps, based on what actually happened during the project. The tech stack, up front Area What we ended up with Tried / abandoned along the way Mobile framework React Native 0.88 + Expo SDK 58 uni-app x (abandoned), Lynx 4.0 (abandoned after a prototype) Routing and compilation Expo Router, React Compiler, TypeScript 6 TypeScript 7 (incompatible with typescript-eslint) Gestures and animation Reanimated 4.7, Gesture Handler 3.3 Builds GitHub Actions: Android APK, iOS upload to TestFlight OTA updates expo-updates protocol, hosted on my own server HarmonyOS Native ArkTS version, builds cleanly in CI Development and debugging Expo Go plus a real device, with the AI driving the phone directly over adb Every "abandoned" and "switched to" in that table was a disagreement between me and the AI. Let's go through them one by one. Gap 1: Say "it's ugly" and the AI can only guess, three rounds in a row When the first version of the UI came out, I said: it's ugly. Round one , Opus 5.5 changed the color scheme. It found three established palettes online and built them into the prototype for me to choose from: Option Source Primary color A Warm Cream Claude's official palette Terracotta orange #c96442 , off-white background #faf9f5 B Teal Radix Sage gray + Jade green #29a383 C Indigo Radix Slate gray + Indigo blue #3e63dd All three palettes were perfectly sensible. I still thought it looked ugly. Round two , it stopped just swapping colors and rebuilt the whole thing in the style of the 2026 Gemini App redesign: pure white or pure black backgrounds, no borders anywhere, an oversized greeting, and a floating pill-shaped input box. In this round it also tracked down a cause I never would have guessed: the screenshots themselves looked cheap. The mockups were captured with headless Chrome on Windows, where Chinese text renders in Microsoft YaHei by default. After switching to Source Han Sans (Noto Sans SC), the look instantly got close to MiSans and PingFang on a phone. Part of what I'd been calling ugly in the first two rounds was really the screenshot font. Round three , I figured the problem might be the icon colors, so I had it drop gradients entirely. It produced six solid-color icon options (black background with a bold sans, black background with a serif, a vermilion seal stamp...), and we settled on a white "Z" on solid black. Only after three rounds did I realize I'd been handing out verdicts the whole time, never direction. If my first sentence had been "conversation-first like ChatGPT, black and white, no gradients," the first version would have been close to final. AI has no aesthetic preferences. What it gives you is the average of a huge number of designs. If you can't articulate what you want, toss it a screenshot of an app you like. That beats ten rounds of "make it look more premium." Gap 2: Whatever the spec says, it does to the letter This project had two computers doing the work: one handled the server and the mobile app, the other handled the Windows client. The AIs on each side didn't share memory. They coordinated through spec documents in the code repository: the protocol, the APIs, what needed to change this time. One side wrote and committed the doc, the other pulled it down, followed it, and marked the status when done. This setup worked really well. When the desktop client got a new icon and was hooked up to the mobile relay, this side wrote the handoff doc first, and the other side just followed it and got it done. But it has a side effect: any decision written into the doc, the AI will carry out without compromise. At one point, the spec switched the mobile tech stack to uni-app x. Opus 5.5 followed it and wrote an entire uni-app codebase, committed it, fixed the issues, and did a beautiful job. Only after it was done did I realize this locked the product into a single platform vendor, DCloud: push notifications, builds, and OTA updates would all depend on them. So I tore it down and started over with React Native + Expo. The AI won't ask on its own, "Will you regret this choice three years from now?" Irreversible decisions like tech stack selection have to be made by a human. Gap 3: Have it write code first, or have it explain why first Later I wanted to try ByteDance's Lynx: one codebase for Android and iOS, and possibly HarmonyOS down the road. Opus 5.5 quickly put together a prototype that compiled, connected to the server, and rendered conversations. But the UI had gone ugly again, nothing like the finalized design. This time I didn't let it jump straight into fixes. Instead I said: no code yet. First let's work out why, then come up with a plan, and only then write code. The reasons it gave were very specific: Area React Native version Lynx prototype Why Icons SVG line icons ☰ ＋ ↑ text symbols Lynx can't render SVG out of the box Sidebar Slides in from the left, 84% width, with an overlay Replaced by a full-page list No ready-made drawer or modal components Bottom sheet Picking a computer, confirmation details with screenshots None Same as above Overall Tuned piece by piece against the prototype Thrown together in an hour to prove feasibility Lynx can't use React Native components; only pure logic can be reused On top of that, testing turned up regressions: in Lynx 4.1.0, taps inside a scroll-view didn't fire, and in ReactLynx 0.128 all taps stopped working entirely, so we had to roll back to 4.0.3 and 0.126. Once the reasons were laid out, the decision was easy: stick with React Native. If I'd just said "make the UI look good," it would probably have spent hours re-tuning everything on Lynx, only for us to switch back in the end. The faster AI writes code, the further it runs in the wrong direction. Gap 4: The more power you give it, the clearer the boundaries need to be For on-device testing, I had the AI drive an Android phone directly over adb: tapping buttons, typing text, taking screenshots to check results. That's how a lot of issues surfaced that the desktop prototype simply couldn't reveal: Symptom Cause Fix Keyboard covers the input box With edge-to-edge enabled, the layout didn't make room for the keyboard Switched KeyboardAvoidingView to padding Taps do nothing after the screen dims The first tap gets used to wake the screen Send KEYCODE_WAKEUP before testing Sidebar swipe gesture ends the moment it starts The native ScrollView stole the touch Switched to Gesture Handler's ScrollView, plus a 36dp-wide transparent hit zone along the left edge Long conversations stop halfway when opened During batched layout, the code's own scroll-to-bottom also fired scroll events, which got misread as "the user scrolled up" Only finger drags can change the "at bottom" state Text typed via adb never appears The WeChat keyboard intercepted the input Tap a candidate word to commit it But things did go wrong once: it hit the back button, landed on the phone's home screen, and its next few taps went straight into WeChat and Alipay. No harm done, but it was enough of a wake-up call: an AI that can only chat can only talk; an AI hooked up to tools can verify its own work, and can also cause trouble on its own. The same model performs at a completely different level depending on whether it has tools. How much access to grant, which device to test on, and which apps are off-limits all need to be spelled out up front. Gap 5: Where you review the work determines what you see The screenshot font issue earlier was really a review problem: if you look at results in the wrong environment, even good work gets dismissed. Builds are the same. Android packages built by GitHub Actions were signed with a different debug certificate every time, so installing a new version meant uninstalling the old one first. Committing a fixed debug.keystore to the repo finally solved it. You'd never catch that without installing twice on a real phone. App Store listing assets are an even bigger pile of details: Asset Required dimensions Title artwork 5244 × 2950 or 3840 × 1646 Search result artwork 5244 × 2950, 3840 × 2560, or 1920 × 1280 iPhone 6.3-inch screenshots 1206 × 2622 or 2622 × 1206 The AI got all these dimensions right on the first try, but the sample data in the screenshots only got swapped for neutral content after I looked them over and asked. Then there was the store description. It wrote it based on our real internal use cases, with every feature covered, but describing it that literally would very likely have gotten stuck in review. The AI didn't know that; I did. We ended up reframing it as "use your phone to remotely control and view the AI conversations on your computer," with the subtitle "Remote-control and view the AI on your computer." AI can get things right, but only someone who's been through it knows which things, done right, are actually risky. Gap 6: Do you know what to ask? Late in the project, I asked: "For small UI tweaks from now on, can we just push an update instead of rebuilding every time?" That one question bought me a full OTA update system: using the expo-updates protocol, with update bundles hosted on my own server. runtimeVersion uses the fingerprint policy, so JS-only releases update automatically when the phone opens the app, and only changes to native code require a new build. If I hadn't asked, it wouldn't have done it on its own. Not because it couldn't, but because it didn't know this mattered to me. Likewise, the HarmonyOS version only started because I asked, "Can you build a native HarmonyOS version?" It wrote one in ArkTS that builds cleanly on GitHub Actions, and along the way worked through a few pitfalls you only find by actually doing it: Huawei's ohpm registry frequently returns 503 to GitHub's runners, so retries are needed; imageknife 3.2.8 and above requires API 18, so we had to stay on 3.2.7. AI goes exactly as far as your questions take it. People who know how to ask naturally get more out of it. Gap 7: Are you really using "the same model"? One last fact that often gets overlooked: when two people say "I'm using Opus 5.5," they may not be using the same thing at all. Difference What it actually means Client Web chat, Claude Code, all sorts of wrapper apps, each with a completely different system prompt Tools Whether it can read files, run a terminal, drive a browser or a phone Reasoning effort Thinking levels, fast mode; the same model varies a lot between high and low settings Context 1M context or standard length; whether old conversations get compacted, and what gets lost when they do Route Official API, a cloud provider, or various third-party relays; the version and limits behind them aren't necessarily the same I built Ruzai with Claude Code: it can read and write the entire repository, run commands, call adb, and use GitHub. Comparing that to a one-question-one-answer session in a web chat was never a fair fight. Final thoughts Putting the seven gaps side by side: Feels "dumb" Feels "smart" Aesthetics Just says "it's ugly" Gives reference screenshots, says clearly what not to do Spec docs Once it's written, it's settled Makes irreversible decisions yourself Order Jumps straight into code Reasons and plan first Tool access None, or wide open Gives tools, and draws boundaries Review Looks at screenshots on a computer Checks on a real device, with real fonts and real data Questions Waits for it to think of things Knows what to ask Setup Only looks at the model name Looks at client, tools, effort level, route Across the whole project, Opus 5.5 wrote nearly all the code, but every turning point was a human decision: dropping uni-app x, passing on Lynx, removing gradients, rewriting the store copy, adding OTA updates. So next time you feel like the AI has "gotten dumber," don't rush to switch models. Take another look at the job description you gave it, and ask whether that was the part that wasn't very smart. For the more technical side of things, like retrieval, context curation, reasoning budgets, and verification, I wrote about those in Before Switching Models, Make Your AI Smarter . The two pair well together. If you're also building your own product with Claude Code or another AI, I'd love to chat: linktr.ee/weiyii Cover image: Crew , CC0 . title: Want smarter AI? Don't rush to change models
author: weiyi
summary: What frustrates me about AI is not knowing when I can rely on it. It explains a complicated problem convincingly, then repeatedly gets a small change wrong. You've supplied the information, yet it overlooks it. It says the code is fixed; run it and the problem is still there. The natural reaction is to blame the model and buy a more expensive one. That might help. But I'd first check whether it received the right information, whether its working process makes sense, and how it decides its work is correct. Leave those unresolved and a stronger model may stumble in exactly the same place. The document is there. Why can't it find it? Connecting AI to a knowledge base is common now. Split documents into chunks, turn them into vectors, store them in a database, retrieve a few relevant passages for a question, then ask the model to answer. That's retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG. It sounds straightforward. The trouble often starts at “retrieve a few relevant passages.” Ask about the specific error code TS-999 , for instance, and the system returns generic troubleshooting articles. Related material, yes, but the answer is missing. Vector search understands meaning; error codes, product models and API names also need exact matching. I'd consider combining semantic search with BM25 keyword search, merging and deduplicating the results, then using a reranker to select the useful passages. There's a subtler problem, too: splitting a document can strip away its meaning. Suppose a retrieved passage says, “This version does not support bulk imports.” Which product? Which version? An obsolete release or the one we're using? Without that background, the model can easily apply the statement to the wrong thing. Adding the title, version, section and necessary context to each passage helps. In Anthropic's experiments, contextualized chunks combined with hybrid retrieval and reranking reduced the top-20 retrieval failure rate from 5.7% to 1.9% . That doesn't promise the same improvement for every knowledge base. What it does suggest is this: when an answer is wrong, check what information the AI actually received first. If retrieval missed the right material, polishing the prompt won't easily rescue the answer. A longer conversation doesn't necessarily mean it understands you better Many people keep everything in one chat: project background, error logs, passing ideas and old plans. After dozens of turns, it feels as though the model should understand them better. But the conversation may now contain conflicting instructions. Last week the plan was A; yesterday it became B. An earlier direction was discussed and later abandoned. A person would need to sort that out, too. The earlier Lost in the Middle study found that, for the models and tasks it tested, putting key information in the middle of long inputs often produced worse results than placing it at the beginning or end. That cannot simply be generalized to every current model. Still, accepting a long input and using all of it well are different abilities. Context engineering sounds technical. In day-to-day work, a large part of it is deciding what the AI needs to see at this particular step. For a website indexing problem, start with robots.txt, the sitemap, page responses and the webmaster dashboard. Read the relevant logs when they're needed. There's no reason to load the whole codebase and every previous conversation at the start. Partway through a long task, leave a handoff: decisions made, files changed, checks passed and unresolved issues. I'd rather it continue from an accurate progress note than guess our current goal from an enormous conversation history. Compression shouldn't mean removing everything, though. Lose a critical constraint and you'll still have to redo the work. Is paying for more thinking worthwhile? Test-time compute studies how additional computation while answering can improve a model's results. It might try several solutions and select among them, or generate an answer and revise it using feedback. Research shows that, on particular tasks and under particular compute budgets, allocating this computation well can let a smaller model outperform a much larger one. How you search and how you judge the candidates both matter. The easy mistake is confusing more thinking with more talking. An answer twice as long isn't necessarily better. Generate five proposals and you still need a way to choose the reliable one. Run tests for code, substitute a calculation back into the original problem, and compare factual claims with primary sources. That feedback gives the next attempt something useful to work with. If what's missing is current pricing or recently updated API documentation, look it up first. Reasoning cannot supply a fact the model never received. I'd prioritize speed for organizing, classifying and extracting information. For difficult reasoning or important code changes, I'd increase the reasoning budget and prepare a way to check the result. The spending worth making is the spending that reduces errors and rework. Give AI real results to check I'm interested in agent harnesses: the surrounding arrangements for splitting tasks, using tools, preserving progress and checking outcomes. In March 2026, Anthropic described an experiment separating planning, generation and evaluation. The generator built an application; the evaluator interacted with running pages, checked APIs and data, then returned specific issues for revision. One detail deserves attention: cost. In one game-editor example, the solo agent ran for about 20 minutes and cost $9 . The full harness ran for about six hours and cost $200 . It produced a more complete result, but at a much higher cost. I wouldn't conclude that adding agents is automatically better value. The time and budgets weren't remotely equal. The useful lesson is to define completion, inspect the result, and bring back concrete failures to fix. Publishing a blog post, for instance, isn't proved by an upload endpoint returning success. Check that the page opens, the body is complete, the canonical URL is right and language links point to the correct versions. Nor would I rely entirely on “take another look for problems.” Models can grade their own output generously. A second model doesn't automatically become a strict reviewer, either. Acceptance criteria should be specific and, ideally, verifiable through tests, actual page interactions or real data. Set retry and spending limits as well, so a minor issue doesn't keep the system looping all night. Does remembering more mean understanding you better? I don't want to explain my writing style every time, or repeatedly remind an assistant that WeChat articles should go into drafts only. Those are lasting preferences worth remembering. “Don't send this one to WeChat yet,” however, applies to the current task. The system needs to understand scope, rather than cancel all future WeChat work. Research such as Mem0 explores extracting important information from conversations, consolidating it and retrieving it later. The difficult part is that information changes and conflicts. Alongside the content, I'd want a memory to carry its source, date, scope and whether a later decision superseded it. Remember user preferences, but inspect live project state. Server ports, dependency versions and deployments should come from the current environment when possible, not a conversation from two weeks ago. I'd reserve fine-tuning for relatively stable, recurring needs: fixed classifications, output formats and particular domain tasks. Frequently changing material belongs in retrieval; live state belongs in tool results. Each has a job. I'd start with the tasks that failed These techniques can all help. They don't all need installing at once. I'd collect twenty or thirty real tasks and record how the AI failed. Can't find the material? Improve retrieval. Forgets requirements late in a task? Organize context and handoffs. Has the facts but reasons badly? Consider a stronger model or more inference compute. Claims completion without finishing? Add verification. Change one or two things at a time, then compare the same tasks: success rate, cost, waiting time and manual cleanup. Keep some tasks out of the tuning process, too, to see whether improvements hold for unfamiliar questions. Otherwise, a better-looking prompt may simply be overfitted to a few examples. My expectations for smarter AI are practical: something that needed five explanations now needs two; work that used to require a complete recheck now arrives with verification. Model upgrades are worth following. There's already plenty to improve while waiting for the next one.
